precepts.text: A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow. Because that man will get people hurt and get people killed.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.

note.label: From Brother To Betrayer

precepts.why:
“A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow.”

Why is he a maul, a sword and a sharp arrow? Because that man will get people hurt, and will get people killed. A false witness is a weapon.

That is what Simon’s false witness against Onias became. He called the high priest a traitor, and before long “by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. His lie was a sword in the hands of his faction, and it drew blood among his own people.

precepts.text: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter. When God conceals something in parables, metaphors, and allegories, it is our job to figure out what the Lord means.
precepts.point: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. Our job is to search the scriptures. The nations do not search the scriptures; they leave their searching from Matthew to Revelation with their misunderstanding through Christianity. If you start from Genesis, you find out that salvation and rulership of the earth is for the Israelites through Christ.

note.label: The Madmen Of China And Their Hatred For Black People

precepts.why:
“It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.” When God conceals something, it is in parable form, metaphors and allegories, and it is our job to figure out what the Lord means by A, B and C.

That is why we must search. Read Jeremiah 48, “against Moab”, or Jeremiah 49, “Concerning the Ammonites”, and unless you search the scriptures and pray to the Lord, you'll say, I don't know who Moab is, I don't know who the Ammonites are, I don't know who Gad is, I'm confused, so I'll stick to Matthew through Revelation. That's what the churches do. Christians don't know and Muslims don't know, confused and discombobulated, unable to identify these nations today.

The honour of kings is to search it out: to find who Moab, Ammon, Gad and Asia are today. The matter is concealed, but it is there for those who search.

precepts.text: A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways: you hear it in his speech and daily decisions, and he is not ready to be hopped behind.
precepts.point: Never aim down spiritually: a sister of years teaching a novice husband to wear his fringes daily will lose respect for him and go elsewhere for understanding, and that is marrying down.

note.label: Why Do Fools Fall In Love

precepts.why:
James puts it in one line: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.” That is the man of Proverbs 25:28, the man who “hath no rule over his own spirit”, a city “broken down, and without walls.” He is cast about, blown to and fro with every wind of doctrine, and a double mind is what keeps him unstable.

Sisters, these are the things to look for. You see the signs. You hear it in his speech and in his daily decision-making. He doesn't know if he is coming or going: one minute it's this, the next minute it's that. He has something brand new he is trying to bring out, like mashed potatoes on the Passover, and you know it did not come from leadership. Red flag. And when he fixes it, sister, you better run.

This is the man you are going to hop behind and expect to make sure everything is taken care of? You mess around and be homeless, trying to figure it out. He is not ready yet. He is unstable.

So when looking for a husband, ask: does this man have stability, does he have discipline? A man with no rule over his spirit is not mentally sound, and he cannot take care of you. Aim up, never down: look for a man with more understanding than you, who can lead you and guide you.

precepts.text: Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee; the honey goes into your food, and the lesson is moderation.
precepts.point: The honey teaching carries a dietary lesson: hast thou found honey, eat so much as is sufficient for thee. Do not overeat; balance your salts, sugars, meats, and dainties moderately.

note.label: Joshua 5: Circumcision of the Flesh and of the Heart

precepts.why:
The honey teaching carries a dietary lesson: “Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it.” The honey goes into your food, your vegetation, and the lesson is moderation.

Do not overeat; balance your salts, sugars, meats, and dainties moderately. Even in a land that floweth with milk and honey, eat so much as is sufficient for thee.

precepts.text: Go and tell your brother his fault between you and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother.
precepts.point: If you reveal the secret, the one who hears it will put you to shame and your bad reputation will not turn away, because now your business is put out there.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
“Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another”. Debating your cause with your neighbor himself means going to him directly.

Christ teaches the same order: “Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.” Tell him his fault between you and him alone, and if he hears you, you have gained your brother. The matter stays between the two of you.

Go to the neighbor himself, not to a third party. That is how a cause is debated without the secret getting out and shame turning back on you.

precepts.text: A tale-bearer reveals secrets, but a faithful spirit conceals the matter.
precepts.point: If you reveal the secret, the one who hears it will put you to shame and your bad reputation will not turn away, because now your business is put out there.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
“Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another: Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away.” One who reveals a secret to another is a gossiper, a backbiter, a tale-bearer.

Solomon names him: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.” You want to be able to trust that what you share is not repeated by others; that is the faithful spirit that conceals the matter, and the talebearer is the opposite.

If you reveal the secret, the one who hears it will put you to shame and your bad reputation will not turn away, because now your business is put out there. Take the cause to your neighbor himself and keep the matter concealed.

precepts.text: Bring back your enemy's ox or ass going astray, and help even the ass of him that hates you lying under his burden.
precepts.point: David showed this with Saul: he cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave but would not kill the Most High's anointed, and Saul confessed David was more righteous, rewarding good for evil. The coals of fire are the shame that comes on such an enemy.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
“If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink”. This is not talking about our natural enemies of the other nations. This is about an enemy among your own people.

The law says the same thing: “If thou meet thine enemy’s ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again. If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, and wouldest forbear to help him, thou shalt surely help with him.” Even your enemy's ox or ass going astray you bring back; even the ass of him that hates you, lying under his burden, you help. Bread and water for the hungry enemy is the same law.

These are commandments given only to Israel, to be taught to our children, so the enemy in view is one among your people. Do him good, and the Most High will reward you.

precepts.text: He appointed a law in Israel commanded to our fathers, to be made known to the children so they set their hope in the Most High and keep his commandments.
precepts.point: David showed this with Saul: he cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave but would not kill the Most High's anointed, and Saul confessed David was more righteous, rewarding good for evil. The coals of fire are the shame that comes on such an enemy.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
Feeding the hungry enemy and giving the thirsty enemy water is a commandment, and the commandments were given to one people. “For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children: That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children: That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments”.

The law was appointed in Israel and commanded to our fathers, to be made known to the children so they set their hope in the Most High and keep his commandments. It is the law among Israel, generation to generation.

That settles who the enemy of Proverbs 25:21 is. This is not our natural enemies of the other nations; it is an enemy among your own people, dealt with by the law given only to Israel and taught to our children.

precepts.text: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them that despitefully use and persecute you.
precepts.point: David showed this with Saul: he cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave but would not kill the Most High's anointed, and Saul confessed David was more righteous, rewarding good for evil. The coals of fire are the shame that comes on such an enemy.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
“If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink”. Christ says the same: “Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you”.

Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them that use you and persecute you. Bread and water for the hungry and thirsty enemy is doing good to them that hate you.

This concerns the enemies among your people, not the other nations. Prayers for vengeance in Luke 18 and Psalm 149 are for our natural enemies; the enemy you feed, bless and pray for is one of your own.

precepts.text: David cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave but would not harm the Most High's anointed.
precepts.point: David showed this with Saul: he cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave but would not kill the Most High's anointed, and Saul confessed David was more righteous, rewarding good for evil. The coals of fire are the shame that comes on such an enemy.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
David showed what it is to do good to an enemy among your own people. Saul was hunting him, and “he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave.” His men told him, “Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee.”

David had Saul in his hand. “Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily.” He cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave, but would not kill the Most High's anointed.

That is bread for the hungry enemy: the enemy in your hand, and you spare him. And the coals of fire on his head are the shame that comes on such an enemy when he learns what you could have done and did not.

precepts.text: Saul wept and said David was more righteous, for David rewarded him good where Saul rewarded evil.
precepts.point: David showed this with Saul: he cut off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave but would not kill the Most High's anointed, and Saul confessed David was more righteous, rewarding good for evil. The coals of fire are the shame that comes on such an enemy.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
After David spared him in the cave, “Saul said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept. And he said to David, Thou art more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil.”

Saul wept and confessed David was more righteous, rewarding good for evil. Those are the coals of fire heaped on the enemy's head: the shame that comes on such an enemy when good is returned for his evil.

“For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord shall reward thee.” David gave good to an enemy among his own people, Saul was put to shame by it, and the Lord rewarded David. That is the proverb lived out.

precepts.text: Better to live with a lion or a dragon than to keep house with a wicked woman.
precepts.point: It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop than with a brawling woman in a wide house. No mansion is big enough to share with a woman who chest-bumps, gets in her man's face, and is shalom at the school but calls a man out of his name at home.

note.label: Proverbs 25: The Proverbs of Solomon Copied by Hezekiah's Men

precepts.why:
“It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house.” No mansion is big enough to share with a woman who chest-bumps, gets in her man's face, and is shalom at the school but calls a man out of his name at home.

Ecclesiasticus says it stronger: “I had rather dwell with a lion and a dragon, than to keep house with a wicked woman.” Better to live with a lion or a dragon than to keep house with a wicked woman. The corner of the housetop and the lion's den are the same choice: anywhere but a wide house with a brawling woman.
